hero.headline: Sebastian man arrested in West Virginia for Vero Beach homicide after license plate readers track multi-state flight
hero.teaser: Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, of Sebastian was arrested Wednesday night by U.S.
hero.body:
Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, of Sebastian was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia and faces a first-degree murder charge in the shooting death of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, in Vero Beach on Sunday morning, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges locally.

Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures. Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead. Investigators classified her death as a domestic violence homicide. Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that the victim had recently ended things with the suspect. She had told her co-workers that if Waggle called or showed up, she wanted nothing to do with him.

According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from West Virginia to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic's Vero Beach home Sunday morning. The sheriff said Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area after the shooting. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene. After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia. Investigators said Waggle left the firearm used in the shooting and other evidence near the scene in Vero Beach. The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle's ex-wife.

The sheriff's office real-time crime center played a crucial role in tracking Waggle's movements across state lines. Detectives determined that Waggle's ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location. U.S. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. His ex-wife was also taken into custody at the scene and is cooperating with investigators. Flowers credited the department's license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest. Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday's announcement.

cards.headline: Florida school camera lawsuits face dismissals as judges side with automated enforcement systems
cards.teaser: Legal challenges to automated school bus and school zone cameras that have generated more than 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in fines across Florida are hitti
cards.body:
Legal challenges to automated school bus and school zone cameras that have generated more than 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in fines across Florida are hitting roadblocks as judges dismiss cases and rule against drivers contesting tickets. Miami-based Attorney Gino Moreno filed three lawsuits last year after drivers hit with $225 school bus camera fines had no way to challenge their citations because the cameras started operating without proper due process in place. Since then, a judge dismissed his federal case in Polk County, a revised complaint remains pending in Miami-Dade, and a Hillsborough County case filed on behalf of client Stanley Shultz awaits a decision on whether it will move forward.

Shultz, who lives in Plant City, was fined for illegally passing a school bus even though video from his citation shows the bus warning lights never flashed. Shultz appealed the fine, but a judge in Tallahassee upheld it despite state law requiring appeals must be heard by local hearing officers. Shultz is now accusing the county of not following state rules for appeal hearings. Legal questions extend beyond school buses to school speed zone cameras, with drivers fined when school was not in session or when signs directing them to slow down when flashing never flashed.

Questions have also emerged about the camera devices themselves. The radar inside the cameras, which state law requires to be approved by the state, is not approved. The state maintains it is exempt. Attorney Ira Karmelin with The Ticket Clinic has successfully used that argument to get school speed zone tickets thrown out, but judges are now starting to side with the state claim of exemption, even though the exemption refers to a radar design, not the device itself.

Since the cameras began operating in Florida, they have generated well over 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in paid fines as of earlier this year. While these legal challenges continue to hit roadblocks, judges have left the door open for appeals or new legal arguments. Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone and photojournalist Matthew Apthorp have been tracking the problems with these automated school cameras for nearly three years.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested on sexual activity with minor charges after SWAT operation
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police arrested Virgil Jason Vinz early Thursday after executing a search warrant at a home on SW Jaslo Avenue.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested Virgil Jason Vinz early Thursday morning after executing a search warrant at a residence in the 900 block of SW Jaslo Avenue. During the operation, Vinz was taken into custody on an arrest warrant without injury. Vinz is charged with five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor.

The police response drew attention from nearby residents, some of whom reported hearing sounds they believed were gunfire. According to the department, the noises were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices, commonly used by SWAT teams during certain tactical operations. Authorities said the devices were deployed by the Port St. Lucie Police Department SWAT Team while officers carried out the warrant.

The department emphasized that the case remains an active and ongoing investigation. Additional information is expected to be released when authorities determine it is appropriate.

Martin County Fire Rescue crews responded to a collision between an SUV and Brightline train Thursday morning in Hobe Sound, leaving one person injured. The man driving the SUV sustained traumatic injuries and was taken to a local hospital. Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies also responded to the scene, and are working to determine the cause of the collision. All train tracks in the area have since been reopened following the incident.

cards.headline: St. Petersburg investor cuts $41,000 in annual costs by replacing contractors with AI
cards.teaser: A Florida real estate investor says artificial intelligence handles nearly every administrative task in his one-person operation, from marketing to bookkeeping.
cards.body:
Alex Jandick, owner of 131 Cash Home Buyers in St. Petersburg, now relies on an AI agent called Claude to handle nearly every administrative task in his one-person operation, saving him more than $41,000 a year. Before making the switch, Jandick was paying $2,500 a month for marketing and nearly $1,000 a month for a bookkeeper. Claude currently handles both for $100 a month. After spending about two weeks setting up and fine-tuning the system, Jandick said the results were immediate.

Jandick says he and Claude essentially split the workload. A human still has to verify the information and input the correct prompts. Jandick is the sole employee of his company, meaning no workers were displaced when he made the switch. After posting online about his AI-driven savings, he faced criticism. According to the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report, AI will displace 92 million jobs globally by 2030. However, the same report projects 170 million new roles will open up, a net gain of 78 million jobs worldwide. A separate 2026 Goldman Sachs study estimates 300 million jobs globally are exposed to automation by AI.

cards.headline: Indian River County Sheriff's Office uses Flock license plate cameras in search for homicide suspect
cards.teaser: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers showed how the agency's Real Time Crime Center is using Flock license plate cameras as investigators search for Matthew Waggle, a person of interest in a Vero Beach homicide.
cards.body:
Sheriff Eric Flowers credited the Indian River County Sheriff's Office Real Time Crime Center and a network of license plate readers with helping investigators piece together Matthew Waggle's movements and locate him in West Virginia. Flowers said the technology was critical to the rapid arrest in the Vero Beach homicide case.

For everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this, the sheriff said during a Thursday news conference. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system. The sheriff clarified that Flock is one brand of automated license plate reader used by law enforcement. Weve made so many cases, and weve protected this community as a result of this, and this is just another example of that, he said.

cards.headline: Kuhio Aloy hits first two pro homers as St. Lucie Mets fall 7-3 to Jupiter
cards.teaser: Kuhio Aloy hit the first two home runs of his professional career Sunday, but the St. Lucie Mets fell 7-3 to the Jupiter Hammerheads to close out a difficult road series.
cards.body:
Kuhio Aloy hit the first two home runs of his professional career Sunday, but the St. Lucie Mets could not overcome a late surge by the Jupiter Hammerheads in a 7-3 loss at Roger Dean Chevrolet Stadium.

The defeat ended a difficult six-game series for St. Lucie, with Jupiter winning five of the six games. The Mets have now lost seven of their last eight.

Aloy, the Mets' 11th-round pick out of Arkansas, provided the offensive highlight for St. Lucie with a pair of solo home runs.

His first came in the second inning and gave the Mets a 1-0 lead. Aloy went deep again in the sixth, tying the game 2-2.

Jupiter slugger Echedry Vargas answered with another big performance of his own. Vargas hit a two-run homer off Candido Cuevas in the fourth inning to put the Hammerheads ahead 2-1.

After Aloy tied the game in the top of the sixth, Vargas responded in the bottom half with a towering solo home run off Conner Ware, putting Jupiter back in front 3-2.

It was Vargas' second multi-homer game of the series. He finished the six-game set with five home runs and now leads the Florida State League with 21 this season. Vargas is the first Hammerheads player to reach at least 20 home runs in a season since Marcell Ozuna in 2012.

Jupiter pulled away with three runs in the seventh inning. One run scored on a groundout and another came home on an error before Jeremy Almonte delivered an RBI double off Jose Guevara, stretching the Hammerheads' lead to 6-2.

The Mets attempted to rally in the ninth after Jupiter reliever Ian Medina walked four batters. Elian Peña drew a bases-loaded walk to force home a run and cut the deficit to 7-3.

Davidxon Lara then entered for Jupiter and retired John Smith III on a groundout with the tying run at the plate to end the game.

Mets starter Will Watson, who is working his way back from an oblique injury on a Minor League Baseball rehab assignment, pitched three scoreless innings.

St. Lucie finished the day at 17-30 in the second half and 50-63 overall.

The Mets are off Monday before returning home Tuesday to begin a six-game series against the Lakeland Flying Tigers at Clover Park in Port St. Lucie. First pitch for Tuesday's opener is scheduled for 6:10 p.m.

hero.headline: Florida school camera lawsuits face dismissals as judges side with automated enforcement systems
hero.teaser: Legal challenges to automated school bus and school zone cameras that have generated more than 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in fines across Florida are hitti
hero.body:
Legal challenges to automated school bus and school zone cameras that have generated more than 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in fines across Florida are hitting roadblocks as judges dismiss cases and rule against drivers contesting tickets. Miami-based Attorney Gino Moreno filed three lawsuits last year after drivers hit with $225 school bus camera fines had no way to challenge their citations because the cameras started operating without proper due process in place. Since then, a judge dismissed his federal case in Polk County, a revised complaint remains pending in Miami-Dade, and a Hillsborough County case filed on behalf of client Stanley Shultz awaits a decision on whether it will move forward.

Shultz, who lives in Plant City, was fined for illegally passing a school bus even though video from his citation shows the bus warning lights never flashed. Shultz appealed the fine, but a judge in Tallahassee upheld it despite state law requiring appeals must be heard by local hearing officers. Shultz is now accusing the county of not following state rules for appeal hearings. Legal questions extend beyond school buses to school speed zone cameras, with drivers fined when school was not in session or when signs directing them to slow down when flashing never flashed.

Questions have also emerged about the camera devices themselves. The radar inside the cameras, which state law requires to be approved by the state, is not approved. The state maintains it is exempt. Attorney Ira Karmelin with The Ticket Clinic has successfully used that argument to get school speed zone tickets thrown out, but judges are now starting to side with the state claim of exemption, even though the exemption refers to a radar design, not the device itself.

Since the cameras began operating in Florida, they have generated well over 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in paid fines as of earlier this year. While these legal challenges continue to hit roadblocks, judges have left the door open for appeals or new legal arguments. Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone and photojournalist Matthew Apthorp have been tracking the problems with these automated school cameras for nearly three years.

cards.headline: St. Petersburg investor cuts $41,000 in annual costs by replacing contractors with AI
cards.teaser: A Florida real estate investor says artificial intelligence handles nearly every administrative task in his one-person operation, from marketing to bookkeeping.
cards.body:
Alex Jandick, owner of 131 Cash Home Buyers in St. Petersburg, now relies on an AI agent called Claude to handle nearly every administrative task in his one-person operation, saving him more than $41,000 a year. Before making the switch, Jandick was paying $2,500 a month for marketing and nearly $1,000 a month for a bookkeeper. Claude currently handles both for $100 a month. After spending about two weeks setting up and fine-tuning the system, Jandick said the results were immediate.

Jandick says he and Claude essentially split the workload. A human still has to verify the information and input the correct prompts. Jandick is the sole employee of his company, meaning no workers were displaced when he made the switch. After posting online about his AI-driven savings, he faced criticism. According to the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report, AI will displace 92 million jobs globally by 2030. However, the same report projects 170 million new roles will open up, a net gain of 78 million jobs worldwide. A separate 2026 Goldman Sachs study estimates 300 million jobs globally are exposed to automation by AI.
